title: Windows toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6)
hook: Daniel keeps praying three times a day, windows open toward Jerusalem, lions or not
tomorrow: They that be wise shall shine (Daniel 12:3)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hand wrote on a palace wall, and Daniel read it: tekel, weighed, and found wanting. Your line was weighed in the balance. What did you put in the pan? Day eight hundred seventy-two.

The trap is a law. Under a new king, Darius, Daniel rises so high that the other officials go looking for something to accuse him of, and find nothing. So they say, in the King James words: "We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God." They go to the king with a flattering idea. For thirty days, let no one ask a petition of any god or any man except the king. Whoever does goes into the den of lions. The king signs it, under the law of the Medes and Persians, which can't be changed. The trap is set. Everyone knows what Daniel does every day.
screen: `NO FAULT BUT HIS FAITH.` → `A LAW FOR THIRTY DAYS.` → `SIGNED, AND IT CAN'T CHANGE.`

segments.voice: Here is what he does: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't close the windows. He doesn't switch to praying in secret for a month. He doesn't march into the square to make a point either. He goes home, to his own room, and does what he did yesterday. As he did aforetime. The courage in this story looks like a habit. And notice which way the windows face. Toward Jerusalem, a city far away. He can't see it. He faces it anyway. The officials catch him, the king, who doesn't want this, tries until sundown to save him and can't, and Daniel goes into the den. At dawn the king runs to the stone and calls. Daniel answers: "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me." This chapter left marks on Jewish prayer. Jewish tradition sets prayer for morning, afternoon and evening, said facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud, in tractate Berakhot, learns from this very verse that a person should pray in a room with windows.
screen: `HE DOESN'T CLOSE THE WINDOWS.` · `AS HE DID AFORETIME.` · `FACING A CITY HE CAN'T SEE.` · then, large: `HIS WINDOWS BEING OPEN TOWARD JERUSALEM.` · then: `THE LIONS' MOUTHS SHUT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a window open, the way Daniel kept his. If there's a window near you, turn toward it, or open it a little. If there isn't, turn toward the light in the room. Daniel faced a city he couldn't see. Let the window stand for whatever you face toward each day: a place, a hope, a person, God. Breathe in the air from outside. If you pray, this is your time, in words from your tradition or in silence, the way Daniel did it in his own room. If you don't, simply sit facing out, and let the day come in. The bell holds the time.
Jerusalem. The city Daniel's open windows faced, three times a day, lions or not, as he did aforetime. Today's word.
Your line: as he did aforetime. Today, keep one daily habit exactly on time, even if the day pushes against it. Day eight hundred seventy-two.

screen: `DAY 872 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THEY THAT BE WISE SHALL SHINE.`

howItsDone: Jewish tradition sets three services a day, Shacharit in the morning, Minchah in the afternoon and Maariv in the evening, facing toward Jerusalem, and the Talmud (Berakhot 31a) learns from Daniel 6 that one should pray in a room with windows.

options: pray quietly with the windows shut until it blows over.
go home and pray as you always have, windows open.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a man who wasn't eaten by lions.
what it means: a man keeps his daily prayer exactly as before, windows open toward Jerusalem, even when it's against the law.
what a scholar hears: Jewish prayer still carries it: three times a day, facing Jerusalem, and the Talmud's rule to pray in a room with windows.
